runs.text: Made by Arshad · 28-fund review
Where each of the 28 funds stands

Nine funds are heavily exposed to an AI-led sell-off, but AI is not the only threat. Oil lurching on every Iran headline (about $96 on 13 Nov, down from $115 in late October), a yen at almost 160 per dollar, the level that has triggered intervention, a 10-year US yield back above 5% with a December Fed hike close to certain, and rising tension around Taiwan each hit different funds. Combining all of these, 11 funds rate High or Very high overall risk. Only the money market funds and cash are close to safe in every scenario.
Why these 28:

together they form a comprehensive set covering cash in three currencies, government and corporate bonds, developed and emerging-market shares, real estate, commodities, gold and absolute return, across the US, Europe, the UK, Japan, Asia and the Pacific. Almost any market event shows up somewhere in the list.

Update · Sat 14 Nov 2026, 6 am Manila (covers Friday 13 Nov in Asia and the US session to mid-afternoon, US time)
Chip stocks slide again as NVIDIA's leadership crisis drags on; US producer prices are still up 6.5% on a year

Chip stocks fell again on Friday. The chip index was down about 3.7% and AMD about 10.6%, as worries about NVIDIA's leadership turned into worries about the whole industry. NVIDIA fell about 2–4% and is heading for a sixth straight weekly fall. In mid-afternoon trading (US time) the S&P 500 was about 0.5–0.8% lower, near 7,530–7,555, roughly 3.4% below its record, though still up about 2% for the week. October producer prices rose 0.3%, a little below forecasts, but are up 6.5% on a year. The 10-year Treasury yield touched 5.17%. Oil and gold were steady. Final US closes were not yet published at writing. No fund rating changes.

cells.text: What happened
Funds affected
What it means
Chip stocks slid again; NVIDIA heads for a sixth weekly fall.

The Philadelphia chip index fell about 3.7% and the tech sector about 1.6%, the worst of the 11 sectors (Reuters via MarketScreener). AMD fell about 10.6% after rising almost 50% the week before, and Broadcom about 5–6%, as early hopes that customers would switch to NVIDIA's rivals gave way to worry about the whole industry (Motley Fool, AP). NVIDIA was down about 2–4% and set for six weekly falls in a row, its longest run since 2012. The Financial Times reported that NVIDIA's board approached Arm's CEO Rene Haas about the top job, and a Senate committee has asked Jensen Huang to testify on 3 Dec (TheStreet). Goldman Sachs said AI investment growth may peak in early 2027 (Yahoo Finance).

The AI-heavy funds (6, 3, 4, 13, 19) lose on two fronts: NVIDIA itself and now its rivals. Tuesday's NVIDIA results are the next big test. Asian chip exposure (24, 22) held up better on Friday, but would follow if US chip stocks keep sliding.
Producer prices came in a touch cooler, but yields kept rising.

October producer prices rose 0.3% in the month against 0.4% expected, but are up 6.5% on a year, the biggest annual rise since November 2022; core producer prices are up about 5.0% (Yahoo Finance, TheStreet). The 10-year Treasury yield rose to about 5.14% after touching 5.17%, its highest since October, while the 2-year was steady near 4.84–4.86% (AP). CME FedWatch shows a December hike of at least a quarter point as fully priced, with about 10% odds of a half point (Reuters via MarketScreener). Fed officials Goolsbee, Daly and Collins all signalled more work to do on inflation.

Still no relief for the bond funds (28, 26, 25, 9) or listed real estate (2): long yields are near their highest since October. The cash and money market funds (14, 10) keep benefiting as a December hike looks certain.
Asia was mixed; Taiwan bounced and the yen sat just below 160.

Taiwan rose 1.7% and TSMC 0.9%. Japan's Nikkei rose 0.8% to 61,283.16, while SoftBank Group fell 5.2%. Korea's KOSPI fell 0.5% to 5,317.05, Hong Kong's Hang Seng 0.9% to 23,786.48 and Australia's ASX 200 0.7% to 9,084.80; Shanghai rose 0.2%. The dollar edged up to 159.91 yen (AP).

Taiwan's rebound helps Asia ex-Japan (24) and emerging markets (22). The Pacific fund (7) is held back by Australia and Hong Kong. With the yen at almost 160, the level that has triggered intervention before, the yen funds (27, 11) face a sharp move either way.
Oil and gold were steady; bitcoin fell below $70,000.

Brent was mostly unchanged near $95.7–96.2 a barrel and US crude near $88.4–88.9 (AP, TheStreet). Gold was little changed at about $3,883–3,894 an ounce, still near its one-year low (Yahoo Finance). Bitcoin fell about 4% to roughly $68,900, below $70,000 for the first time since August (TheStreet).

A quiet day for the commodity (12) and UK (8) funds, which gain from high oil, and for oil importers (5, 23). Gold miners (1) stay weak with gold stuck near its low. Bitcoin's slide is another sign that speculative money is pulling back.
Coming up (Manila):

Japan Q3 GDP Mon 16 Nov; NVIDIA results Wed 18 Nov, early morning (Tue 17 Nov, US time); Fed minutes Thu 19 Nov, early morning; Anthropic's market debut expected around 19–20 Nov; Jensen Huang asked to testify to the Senate Banking Committee on 3 Dec (US time); US November jobs report Fri 4 Dec, 9:30 pm; Fed decision 8–9 Dec, with a hike fully priced.

NVIDIA's results and Anthropic's debut make next week decisive for the AI-heavy funds (6, 13, 3, 4). Hawkish Fed minutes would add to pressure on the bond funds (28, 26). Weak Japanese GDP would complicate a Bank of Japan hike and weigh on the yen funds (27, 11).

AI-crash scenario
Who gets hurt, who holds

In an AI-led crash I estimate the most AI-concentrated funds could fall 30–40%, broad developed-market equity funds 20–30%, and cash would hold its value. Government bonds would likely gain a few percent, but only if the crash lowers inflation fears rather than arriving with another oil shock.

My estimates from each fund's AI concentration, equity beta and volatility, calibrated to the 2000–02 dot-com bust (S&P 500 about −49%), 2022 (MSCI World −18%, US Treasuries −13%) and Korea's July 2026 chip crash (KOSPI −40% in six weeks). Not forecasts.
Scenario assumed.

AI capital spending is cut sharply, US mega-cap tech falls 40–50%, the S&P 500 falls 25–35% and Asian chip stocks repeat their July 2026 slide. The Fed responds by cutting rates. If inflation stays high instead (for example, the Strait of Hormuz closes again), the bond funds would not rise and only cash would hold.
Liquidity.
Every fund deals daily; settlement is typically 1–3 business days plus any platform processing time. In a crash the practical risks are:
Emerging-market and Asian equity funds (22, 24) and the commodity swap fund (12) can see prices gap and dealing spreads widen.
Funds can apply swing pricing or, in extreme cases, defer large redemptions; this matters most for the active and EM funds.
Selling after a fall locks in the loss. The 2000–02 and 2022 sell-offs both had sharp rebounds that punished late sellers.

Beyond AI
Eight other risks in the news now, and which funds they hit
An AI crash is one way to lose money; these are the others. Several are already moving markets this month. Numbers link to each fund's analysis.

1 · Yen turmoil

The yen fell to about 163 per dollar in late July, prompting a joint US–Japan intervention (Japan reportedly spent around $85bn) that pushed it to 155. By mid-August most of that gain had reversed. Japan had already spent ¥11.7 trillion defending the yen in April–May. It was near 158 on 27 Oct, and Finance Minister Katayama has warned she is ready to act again, with traders watching 160. In the week to 6 Nov the dollar traded between about 157.3 and 158.8 yen; hawkish Bank of Japan minutes and the stock rout helped the yen, but the strong US jobs report pushed the dollar back to the mid-158s. The pressures are a slow Bank of Japan (held at 1.25% on 30 Oct, though it signalled more hikes), PM Takaichi's 19 Oct signal that about ¥10 trillion of tax cuts may be funded with deficit bonds (debt is 204% of GDP), 10-year JGB yields near 3%, and an oil import bill that has only just started to ease (Brent near $98 on 6 Nov, from $115 in late October). On 12–13 Nov the dollar reached about 159.8–159.9 yen, the closest yet to 160. The move can run either way: intervention or a carry-trade unwind could lift the yen 5% in days.

2 · Oil shock and the Strait of Hormuz

Brent settled at $115.32 on 28 Oct, about 75% higher than a year ago. After the 3 Nov US election, Brent fell 8.7% to $94.62 on 4 Nov as markets priced pressure to end the war, and it ended the week of 6 Nov at $98.32, down about 16%, its steepest weekly fall since 2020. On 8 Nov the US launched "Task Force Iron Gate" to curb Iran's trade over land and the Caspian Sea, and on 9 Nov Brent fell about 5% to roughly $93–94, its lowest since 31 Aug. On 10 Nov Brent briefly fell below $90 for the first time since August, ending near $91.8, after Trump said the war was militarily effectively over. On 11 Nov Iran denied talks and said the strait stays shut until its conditions are met; monitors counted at least 37 attacks on ships so far in November, the most of any month in the war. On 12 Nov Trump said the US does not need a deal, clouding a reported Qatari plan to reopen the strait, and Brent rose to about $94–96, where it held on 13 Nov. Nothing is agreed, and the strait has been largely closed since March. This is a two-way risk. A deal could send oil sharply lower; Brent fell to about $72 during the brief June truce. A longer closure keeps inflation and rates high.

3 · Sticky inflation and rising bond yields

US CPI rose to 3.7% in September (core 2.6%). The Fed held on 28 Oct in a 10–2 vote, with both dissenters wanting a hike. The 10-year Treasury yield touched 5.35%, the highest since 2002, and Pimco's CIO has said 6% is possible. On 6 Nov a strong October jobs report (165,000 jobs against about 65,000 expected, unemployment 4.1%) lifted the 2-year yield to 4.51% and the 10-year to 4.86%, and pushed CME odds of a December hike to about 77%. On 10 Nov October CPI rose 0.4% in the month (core 0.3%), above forecasts; the 10-year yield jumped to about 5.01%, a December hike became close to fully priced, and Fed Governor Waller said a half-point move could be considered. On 11 Nov US bond markets were shut for Veterans Day; CME odds still showed a December hike fully priced, with about 13% odds of a half point, and Governor Bowman said there is still work to do on inflation. On 13 Nov October producer prices rose 0.3%, slightly below forecasts but 6.5% higher than a year earlier, the most since 2022; the 10-year yield touched 5.17%, and CME odds of a half-point December hike were about 10%. Rising yields hurt bonds, REITs and expensive growth stocks at the same time, as in 2022, when stocks and bonds fell together.

4 · French debt stress and a weaker euro

France's 10-year yield hit 4.98% on 21 Oct, a 24-year high, and its spread over Germany reached 157 bp, the widest since the euro crisis. EUR/USD fell 3.9% between 9 Sep and 23 Oct even though the ECB raised rates twice this year to 2.50%. Eurozone inflation is 3.8%, and the October PMI fell to a four-month low. On 29 Oct the ECB held, the euro touched a 17-month low, and Lagarde's early exit (7 Feb 2027, before the French election) was confirmed.

5 · Taiwan tension and Asian currency stress

China held live-fire drills across five sea areas on 12–17 Oct, coast-guard ships harassed Taiwanese vessels on 18 Oct, and on 16 Oct Beijing drafted export curbs on about 40 technologies, including AI and chips. On 15 Oct foreign investors sold NT$165bn of Taiwan stocks in one day, Korean outflows for October passed $10bn, the Philippine peso passed 63 per dollar for the first time, and India and Indonesia intervened to support their currencies.

6 · AI debt inside "safe" bond funds

AI-related borrowing has passed roughly $466–500bn this year and makes up about 10% of the largest long-term investment-grade bond ETFs. Oracle's 5-year CDS more than doubled to about 308 bp, Meta's and NVIDIA's hit records in October, and CoreWeave's implies a default probability above 60%. Pimco as a firm bought $18bn of Meta's Hyperion data-centre bond. On 28 Oct Alphabet reported that its long-term debt had jumped from $46.5bn to $125.1bn in a year, alongside $12.4bn of stock sales, to pay for AI. On 2 Nov Oracle filed to sell $10bn of stock and $10bn of senior notes for the same purpose. After the 3 Nov election, analysts flagged Democrats' openness to data-centre moratoriums, and on 4 Nov AI-infrastructure names fell (NVIDIA −3.2%, CoreWeave −9.9%, Vistra −13.8%) even as the market rallied. On 5 Nov the chip index fell 12.3% and the Nasdaq entered correction, as investors priced a slower, costlier AI build-out. On 11 Nov CoreWeave said it expects about $9bn of customer prepayments over three months and plans no more expensive debt through 2027; its shares jumped more than 20% and the chip index about 7%.

7 · UK Budget and gilts

The 10-year gilt yield touched 5.53% on 8 Oct, the highest since 2007. UK inflation is 3.5%, and markets expect a Bank of England hike on 5 Nov. The 28 Oct Budget kept about £15bn of fiscal headroom and gilts held steady, but it doubled the bank surcharge to 6%, a cost for the UK fund's banks.

8 · Gold's correction and Australia's rate hikes

Gold briefly fell below $4,000 on 23 Oct, about a quarter under its January record. It dropped alongside stocks as leveraged investors raised cash, so it did not behave as a safe haven that day. It slipped again on 29 Oct and fell 3.3% to a one-year low of $3,899 on 30 Oct as tech sold off, just above Standard Chartered's $3,886 warning level, then rebounded to $3,957 on 2 Nov and $4,070 on 4 Nov. It gained about 4.5% in the week to 6 Nov, its best week since August, ending near $4,050–4,080. On 12 Nov it fell about 2.9% to roughly $3,885 as the dollar firmed on Fed hike bets. In Australia, the RBA has hiked four times this year to 4.60%, CPI is 4.0%, and Q3 core inflation of 3.7% beat forecasts on 28 Oct, and on 3 Nov the RBA hiked a fifth time to 4.85%, the highest since 2008, in a split 6–3 vote that dropped its tightening bias.

November so far. The 3 Nov midterms, in which Democrats won both houses of Congress, set off the sharpest AI sell-off of the year on worries about slower data-centre building. On 5 Nov the chip index fell 12%, its worst day since 2020, and the Nasdaq entered a correction. In the week to 6 Nov the S&P 500 lost 2.7% and the Nasdaq 3.4% (AP); Japan's Nikkei lost 9.3%, leaving it more than 20% below its June record (Yahoo Finance), and Korea's KOSPI 11.7% (Seoul Economic Daily). Brent fell about 16% on hopes of a US–Iran deal (CNBC), while a strong jobs report kept a December Fed hike likely (InvestmentNews). On 9 Nov Wall Street rebounded: the S&P 500 rose 2.3% and the chip index about 7%, while NVIDIA fell 4.4% on a board probe of its CEO and Brent dropped to about $93–94 (Reuters). On 10 Nov hotter October inflation (0.4% in the month) pushed the 10-year yield to about 5.01% and the S&P 500 down about 0.4%, with NVIDIA down 6.3%; Asia had rallied, with the KOSPI up 4% (AP). On 11 Nov chip stocks rebounded about 7% after CoreWeave's results, lifting the S&P 500 about 1.3% to roughly 7,620 (Reuters). On 12 Nov NVIDIA's CEO Jensen Huang resigned; NVIDIA fell as much as 14% before paring losses, the S&P 500 slipped 0.4% to about 7,592, and Brent rose after Trump said no Iran deal is needed (Kiplinger, AP). On 13 Nov chip stocks slid again (chip index about −3.7%, AMD about −10.6%) and the S&P 500 traded near 7,550 in the afternoon, still up about 2% for the week; October producer prices were up 6.5% on a year (Reuters, AP).

In an inflationary environment stocks and bonds can fall together, as in 2022. If an AI crash instead triggers a growth scare and Fed cuts, Treasuries and high-quality bonds should rally. Which of those two worlds arrives decides whether the bond funds protect you; only the cash-like funds are safe in both.
Fund by fund
Holdings, returns, AI exposure and liquidity
Buying in a sell-off
If the S&P 500 falls 5%, 10% or 20%: which funds to add

A guide to which of the 28 funds tend to be worth adding as a sell-off deepens, using the S&P 500's fall from its 7,819 record (6 Oct 2026) as the trigger, because it is the market's main gauge. The idea is to add the steadier, low-AI funds first and the high-growth, AI-heavy funds only once they are much cheaper. Purchases are funded mainly from cash and from bonds that have risen. Where we are now: in Friday afternoon trading (13 Nov, US time) the S&P 500 was at about 7,550, roughly 3.4% below its record, as chip stocks slid again. It is still above the −5% level (~7,430), which is about 1.6% lower. The −10% level (~7,040) is about 6.8% lower.

These fall most in an AI crash, so they rebound most from a low base. Adding them only after a 20% fall means buying AI at a discount instead of at the peak. REITs recover when the Fed cuts.
Gold miners (1), and anything you may need to sell within 2–3 years

runs.text: Nobody can pick the bottom. Splitting purchases across the three levels means you are never all-in too early or left with all your cash. The dot-com and 2022 sell-offs both had sharp rallies on the way down.

In an AI or growth crash, Treasuries usually rise, so selling some bonds to buy stocks works. In an oil or inflation shock, bonds may fall too: fund purchases from cash (14) instead, and consider trimming the commodity fund (12), which is likely to have risen.
Buying a dip means
switching
part of an existing balance (for example, from Insight into Developed World). Changing only where new money goes keeps buying at every level automatically, but does not move what is already invested.
